tier_reason: The 2026-09-24 native Linux report preserves its harness in docs/reports/2026-09-24-native-linux-x86-64/harness/ (prepare.py compiles md4c with clang -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c99; build.json records Rust opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, -C target-cpu=generic), PROVENANCE.md names Ubuntu clang 18.1.3, and host.txt names the AMD EPYC 7763; md4c 0.31x/0.29x (50 agreeing documents) and 0.24x/0.20x (14 documents) appear in the table.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Native Linux x86-64 report 2026-09-24 (AMD EPYC 7763): md4c reaches 0.31x (fresh) and 0.29x (reuse) of Ferromark v2 throughput on the 50 documents with matching output across five engines, so Ferromark is about 3.2x and 3.4x faster (derived from page data); on the 14 documents where all six engines agree md4c is 0.24x fresh and 0.20x reuse (about 4.2x and 5.0x, derived from page data). Held-out PGO evaluation (28 held-out documents, 24 of them compared with md4c): default builds 3.05x fresh and 3.22x reuse; with PGO applied to the Rust engines only (md4c not PGO-built) 3.84x and 4.02x. Second report, blacksmith Linux x86-64 (2026-10-01, all 57 documents including differing outputs, 'AMD EPYC'): vs md4c 2.95x fresh and 3.06x reuse (md4c marked with an asterisk for differing output), vs cmark 5.70x and 6.25x, vs cmark-gfm 6.15x and 6.67x (Comrak, a Rust sibling, 5.10x and 5.51x).

notes: Numbers and build details check out against the report, PROVENANCE.md, build.json, host.txt and harness/prepare.py; the held-out comparison uses 28 held-out documents of which 24 enter the md4c ratio (the record said 24 documents of held-out half), and the PGO columns favour Ferromark because md4c is not PGO-built. Shortcomings to record: first-party harness on a shared GitHub runner, engines produce different HTML on 7 to 43 of 57 documents, md4c allocations redirected to mimalloc rather than its stock malloc, different parsing algorithms (same_algorithm false), and the blacksmith cmark build log does not show the -O3 line (GNU 13.3.0 confirmed, CMake Release defaults to -O3). README's 'leads every measured library' page (ferromark.dev) was not opened.

corrections.caveats: No comparison against aklomp/base64, Turbo-Base64 or fastbase64 was found. The project's own harness (Nugine/simd-benches) compares base64-simd only against Rust crates, and its published results live on a github.io page that is blocked here. The only C-baseline number is a maintainer's PR comment (uutils/coreutils #8578, 2025-09-08, merged 2025-09-09) with no machine description, no GNU coreutils version and no build flags; the end-to-end CLI time also includes the uutils I/O path (system time 1.937 s against GNU's 0.996 s), so 1.56x understates the encoder gap, while the 1.91x gain over the previous uutils build is a before/after on the same program. GNU base64 is not in the listed baselines (aklomp/base64, Turbo-Base64, fastbase64). The published base64-simd crate is still 0.8.0 (released 2022-12-28); repository commits after that (last 2026-08-30) are not in a crates.io release.

notes: PR #8578 hyperfine output matches the record exactly (4.901 s, 3.146 s, 5.998 s, 1.56 +/- 0.02 and 1.91 +/- 0.03 times faster); I did not see the hyperfine flags quoted, so the record's '-N --warmup 3, 10 runs' is unconfirmed. Shortcomings to record: single maintainer comment without hardware or GNU version, CLI-level comparison mixes in I/O, the win is SIMD versus GNU's scalar routine rather than a language effect, and the listed fast C base64 libraries were never compared.

tier_reason: README hyperfine output shows hunt 180.2 ms vs find 2.219 s (12.31x) and 633.6 ms vs 3.473 s (5.48x); the bench script benchmarks/run is public but no CPU model, GNU find version or hunt version is given, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: README numbers only, measured with hyperfine on one unspecified machine (no CPU, kernel, filesystem, cache state, GNU find version or hunt version) over a tree that includes a network drive and an external drive. hunt is multithreaded while GNU find is single-threaded, and the tools do different work (hunt --first searches [current_dir, home_dir, root] in its own order, sorts and groups output, matches exact or substring names; find -name uses glob matching in depth-first order), so the first-match latency depends on where the file sits in each tool's traversal order. The win is parallelism, not per-thread efficiency: user plus system CPU time is about 1.54 s for hunt against 1.58 s for find in the first-match case and about 5.38 s for hunt against 2.84 s for find in the all-matches case (derived from page data). benchmarks/run runs hyperfine -N --warmup 1, so the timings use a warm dentry and inode cache. The benchmark script is benchmarks/run (for the 'run' task runner), not benchmarks.sh as the README says (benchmarks.sh returns 404), and it compares hunt, a previous hunt 2.3.0 binary, fd and find (no locate). Last commit 2025-07-06 (about 15 months before the check). The locate row was omitted for the second case and quoted as 486.8 ms in the README text.

notes: README numbers match the record. Shortcomings to record: multithreaded tool against single-threaded GNU find (hunt spends equal or more total CPU time), different matching semantics and traversal order, warm-cache timings on one undescribed machine, stale since 2025-07-06.
